title_en.text: Mabitac Church (Nuestra Señora de Candelaria Parish Church)

tagline.text: A 1618 hilltop church above 126 steps, overlooking Laguna de Bay

children.text: Mabitac Church is a parish church built in stone on a hilltop in 1618, formally named Nuestra Señora de Candelaria Parish Church. You climb 126 steps for views of Laguna de Bay and the town, and at the foot of the hill stands a relief commemorating the 1900 Battle of Mabitac.
Mabitac is a small town in the far east of Laguna, in the hills between Siniloan and Pililla. It is said to be about
76km

from Manila, close on the map but a winding road over the hills. A low hill rises in the middle of town, and on top of it stands Nuestra Señora de Candelaria Parish Church, commonly called Mabitac Church. Locals call the hill Kalbaryo (Calvary).

The history of this church begins with its image of Our Lady. According to commonly cited accounts, around 1599–1600 the alferez Cristobal Mercado commissioned an image of Our Lady of Candelaria and donated it to Paco Church; it later passed through a hospital chapel in Los Baños and then to a chapel on the Siniloan side. The people of Mabitac wanted to keep the image, and the most widely told version says it was enthroned here in 1615. Sources differ on the years and the order of events, so for the exact sequence it is safest to follow the parish or the Mabitac municipal office. The first church is said to have stood between two Siniloan barrios; because of frequent flooding, the Franciscans rebuilt it in stone on Calvary Hill in 1618. The parish itself is also recorded as established in 1618.

The present building has a Spanish-style façade of adobe stone. It was badly damaged by the earthquakes of 1880 and 1937 and repaired several times, and the belfry is described as the only surviving original part of the 1618 church. The interior is relatively modern, but the lower part of the two-level retablo holds a 17th-century image of Our Lady of Candles. The façade has niches for three male saints, and a round stained-glass window above the porch shows the town's patroness.

Mabitac also matters as a historical destination. On September 17, 1900, during the Philippine-American War, Filipino forces led by General Juan Cailles defeated American troops at the entrance to the town in the Battle of Mabitac. In the town center below the hill stand a colorful relief commemorating it (the Battle of Mabitac mural) and a marker reading "Labanan sa Mabitac." It is not a flashy tourist attraction, but it is a pleasant, quiet stop on an eastern Laguna church tour.

The stone stairway leading to the church's side entrance is often cited as 126 steps. It reportedly began with 96 steps and was extended later, and sources give different counts. Rest along the way and the town roofs and mountains open up wider as you climb.

blocks.title: Views of Laguna de Bay and the town

children.text: From the yard on top of Kalbaryo Hill you see mountains on one side and the town and the direction of Laguna de Bay on the other. The clearer the day, the farther you see, so going in the morning or late afternoon gives softer light.

Of the church that has survived several earthquakes, only the belfry is known to remain from the original 1618 structure. Rather than looking at the whole building, study the stonework and color of the belfry to sense the Spanish era.
The heart of this church is the 17th-century image of Our Lady of Candles. It is enshrined in the lower part of the two-level retablo, and many devotees come on the parish feast day every February 2.
The façade has niches for three saints, and above the porch a round stained-glass window depicts the town's patroness. For photos, the plaza below is a good spot to capture the whole façade at once.

blocks.title: St. Lorenzo Ruiz and the Stations of the Cross

children.text: In the middle of the yard, a statue of St. Lorenzo Ruiz faces the façade, and the Stations of the Cross are placed around the grounds. It makes for a slow, pilgrim-style walk.

On a platform beside the road at the foot of the hill stands a tall relief dominated by the colors of the Philippine flag. It commemorates the Battle of Mabitac on September 17, 1900, and seeing it before climbing the church steps connects the story of this town.

blocks.title: The Three Kings festival on January 6

children.text: On January 6 Mabitac holds a Three Kings festival that re-enacts the Magi's journey to find the infant Jesus. The schedule and format can change each year, so check announcements from the municipal hall or the parish before you go.

items.title: 1–2 hour route
items.subtitle: From the mural to the church yard

children.text: Arrive in the town center and see the Battle of Mabitac mural and marker at the foot of the hill first. Reading up on the 1900 battle beforehand makes the town look different.
Climb the Kalbaryo Hill steps. There are 126 of them, so feel free to rest halfway. It is better to avoid the strong midday sun.
In the church yard, see the statue of St. Lorenzo Ruiz and the Stations of the Cross, and enjoy the views of the lake and town.
If the doors are open, step inside and quietly see the 17th-century image of Our Lady of Candles. Refrain from taking photos or moving around during Mass.
Take one more look at the belfry and façade, then have lunch at a local eatery or move on to the next church.
The church doors may be closed at some times of day, so timing your visit to Mass hours (see Costs and Tips) makes it easier to go inside.
Set out from Manila by way of Manila East Road or the Marilaque Highway and visit Mabitac first.
Finish your visit to Mabitac Church.
Head toward Pakil and Paete and look around the churches and lakeside towns.
If time allows, continue to Pagsanjan, Liliw and Pila, and finish with kesong puti (white cheese) in Santa Cruz.
Routes linking several churches can involve long travel times between stops, so check local traffic conditions.

items.title: From Manila by car or motorcycle

children.text: Mabitac is said to be about
76km
from Manila. A commonly used route runs along Manila East Road or the Marilaque Highway (Marcos Highway) through Rizal province into Mabitac.
The stretch climbing from Pililla up to Mabitac is steep, and the road down from Mabitac to Pililla is a hard descent. Parts of the road have no street lighting at night, so travel in daylight.
Travel time varies greatly with your starting point and traffic. Check live directions on a map app.

One option is to take a bus or UV Express van from Manila toward eastern Laguna, go to Santa Cruz or Siniloan, and transfer to a jeepney or van bound for Mabitac. No confirmed direct route or fare is available, so check locally.
Mabitac is said to be about
30km
from Santa Cruz.
The church is in the town center (poblacion) and can be reached on foot from the main street. If you take a tricycle, ask the fare before you ride.
The way up to the church is a stairway, so if you carry a lot of luggage, leave it near your vehicle before you climb.
The dry season from November to May is the best time for Mabitac. Since the visit involves stairs and an open yard, the stone steps can be slippery on rainy days.
On the February 2 parish feast and the January 6 Three Kings festival the town is lively but crowded, with congested roads, so for a quiet visit choose a weekday morning.

Mabitac Church is not a glamorous large tourist site but a working parish church that townspeople climb up to every day. So the best way to see it is to stay a little over an hour, taking in the stairs, the views, the belfry, the image of Our Lady and the battle relief slowly. Rather than chasing photos, I recommend a trip of walking and feeling the atmosphere of the town. Korean travelers may even treat the drive itself, from eastern Metro Manila through Rizal, Antipolo and Pililla, as part of the outing.
Mabitac is a small town with few places to stay. Most visitors sleep in nearby towns such as Santa Cruz, Siniloan or Paete and make it a day trip. Check availability and location before you go.

For meals you can use small eateries in the town center or a restaurant near the Pililla boundary (Mang Vic's Eatery is known as a rest stop with a view). Check opening status and menu locally. If you pass through Laguna, local snacks such as kesong puti from Santa Cruz are also worth trying.
The church doors may be closed at times. Going at Mass times (Wed–Fri 6 PM, Sat 7 AM, Sun 6, 8, 10 AM and 5 PM) makes it easier to see the interior, but check the latest announcements.
You climb 126 steps, so wear non-slip sneakers and bring water.
To capture the whole façade at once, shoot from the plaza below.
Seeing the Battle of Mabitac mural at the foot of the hill together with the church makes the town's story continuous.
It is still a working parish church, so modest clothing is better than shorts or sleeveless tops.
Inside the church, remove your hat and lower your voice. If worshippers are praying, do not approach the altar.
The view of Laguna de Bay depends on weather and visibility, so choosing a clear day increases satisfaction. On cloudy days the distant view can look hazy.
The uphill and downhill stretches on the Pililla side are hard for motorcycles and bicycles, so check your brakes and your stamina.
Linking Mabitac with the nearby churches of Pakil and Paete makes a one-day church tour. Allow plenty of travel time.
The church may be closed depending on Mass and time of day, and the roads outside town are dark at night, so travel in daylight.
Refrain from photography and movement during Mass or events, and view quietly.
Stone steps are slippery in the rain, so hold the rail and climb slowly.
There is no confirmed information on transport and fares, so check locally before you travel.
Sources differ on years and the number of steps, so give priority to signboards and the parish's own explanation.
Keep belongings out of sight and be careful in quiet, secluded spots.
Often presented as the next stops on the old-church circuit that runs along the east side of Laguna de Bay from Mabitac. Travel time depends on traffic, so check locally.
A leading attraction visited when continuing the pilgrimage along the Laguna de Bay side.
A town with slipper (tsinelas) workshops and an old church, good for continuing a church tour.
A town of historic buildings, often described as the last stop of the church circuit.
